thread.title: Do you secretly visit McDonald’s or quietly shop at Louis Vuitton? Why guilty pleasures are so hard to give up

author: Andrew Keshner
title: Do you secretly visit McDonald’s or quietly shop at Louis Vuitton? Why guilty pleasures are so hard to give up
text:
One person worried that his Louis Vuitton LVMH, -1.05% merchandise would rankle family members with less money. Another said that his penchant for going to McDonald’s MCD, +0.97% alone gutted a healthy-living image.
These people, who were part of a new study, still bought their luxury goods and fast-food meals. But they just were careful how they went about it.
Embarrassment, conformity and avoiding conflict are some of the reasons people keep certain purchases secret, according to a new study looking into cravings that dare not speak their name.
Whatever the unspoken item, the research said the covert consumer psychology yields a common result: An even stronger bond to the brand than if the buyer was open about buying it.
Whatever the unspoken item, the research said the covert consumer psychology yields a common result: An even stronger bond to the brand than if the buyer was open about buying it. That makes buyers indulging a guilty pleasure a lot like lovers locked in an illicit relationship, said marketing professors Veronica Thomas, associate professor in the Department of Marketing at Towson University, and Robert Jewell, associated professor in the College of Business Administration at Kent State University.
Research says when people are involved in a secret relationship, they try unsuccessfully to squelch the desire, which only increases the fire. The cycle called is “obsessive preoccupation,” noted the peer-reviewed Journal of Consumer Psychology study posted Monday.
When people have a guilty pleasure, whether it’s fast food or luxury goods, “the same cognitive mechanism is occurring,” Thomas, the lead author, told MarketWatch.
Marketers and academics have been aware that consumers keep quiet about buying some totally legitimate, openly sold merchandise, she added. This was illustrated in research on “brand communities” mentioning Star Trek lovers cordoning off their devotion from co-workers.
But Thomas said her research, finding 66% of participants keeping at least one brand a secret, is the first to delve into the prevalence of brand secrecy and the consequences when customers stay quiet about certain buys.
Thomas admits she’s been cagey about certain purchases over the years.
Veronica Thomas confesses to only telling co-workers about her Kate Spade bag and clothes if asked, but she’s more reluctant to divulge that information to her family, lest she be judged for it. For example, she has a Kate Spade TPR, +0.77% bag and clothes and would volunteer that information if a co-worker asked what she was wearing. “With my family, I might talk around the subject,” said Thomas. She would not like her family judging her about how she spends her discretionary income or making them feel uncomfortable about their own finances, she explained.
Study participants confessed to Thomas all sorts of secret loves during her research, she said. For example, one woman told the professor she loved Britney Spears but made sure her heavy metal-loving husband and his friends never saw the pop star’s music.
The study comes as consumers are getting pushed and pulled in different directions on how to handle their hankerings.
Some companies, especially in the fast-food industry, play into covert caloric contentment through loyalty programs that reward repeat customers. But the fast-food industry is also trying to cater to some consumers’ better angels, putting more health-conscious choices on their menus. Some companies have even changed their logos, perhaps, to take the guilty pleasure out of the title: Dunkin’ Donuts DNKN, -1.31% rebranded as simply Dunkin’ earlier this year, removing their key band from the title. The company said it was an attempt to “ modernize ” the brand.
Discreet packaging offering a variety of goods with differing amounts of branding and accessibility on online food ordering were all ways companies could attempt to overcome shoppers guilt, the study found. Then there are companies that want consumers to proudly own their devotion. Bravo, which is owned by Comcast CMCSA, +0.97% a channel with a stable of reality TV shows, including the successful “Real Housewives” franchise, launched an ad campaign earlier this year intended to encourage viewers to come out with their allegiance.
Food and beverages were the second-most discussed items in the study’s survey after clothing. “I think there’s a lot of shame surrounded with unhealthy foods,” she said. Electronics — whether, for example, someone preferred Apple AAPL, -0.65% products — came in third, Thomas said.
The research used several experiments to gauge the surreptitious devotion. One part was a survey of almost 400 participants. Embarrassment (51%) was the most common reason participants said they didn’t mention certain purchases.
For example, one woman said she didn’t tell others she shopped a Torrid, a plus-size brand. “I don’t want anyone to notice I am plus size or be able to guess my clothing size — they might be shocked at how large [it is]. It is embarrassing.”
Other times, consumers don’t want to upset people close to them. One participant on a tight budget was married to someone with a fierce devotion to local business and had a dim view of Walmart WMT, +1.31% and its effects on small competitors. “The fact is, things are just cheaper at Walmart. When I go shopping or need to pick something up, I always go where it’s cheaper if I can be certain that my husband won’t find out.”
For Thomas, one surprising motivator was the effort to maintain exclusivity. “I prefer not to see someone else wearing the same items I am wearing,” said one Vera Wang shopper.
Discreet packaging offering a variety of goods with differing amounts of branding and accessibility on online food-ordering companies, were all ways companies could play to shoppers trying to keep things hush-hush, Thomas said.
The study used several experiments, too. In one, 87 college students told to eat a package of granola that was mailed to them. One group was instructed the granola was a secret food they couldn’t tell others about. The other group had no such instructions.
The group told to eat their granola secretly had a stronger connection to the food, the research said.
Thomas said the study’s findings could let marketers breathe a sigh of relief even as they seek out social media “brand evangelists” to help reach consumers. “This shows it’s okay if you get brand consumption as a secret,” she said.
